What is AJAX and what problem does it solve?

AJAX is a technique, not a library: JavaScript sends HTTP requests in the background (XHR or fetch), gets data (JSON, XML, HTML fragments), and updates part of the DOM. It avoids full page reloads, which makes the app faster and more responsive, keeps UI state (scroll position, form input), and uses less bandwidth. It's what makes SPAs, autocomplete, infinite scroll and live validation possible.
Explain readyState and status in XMLHttpRequest.

readyState tracks the request lifecycle: 0 UNSENT, 1 OPENED, 2 HEADERS_RECEIVED, 3 LOADING, 4 DONE. status is the HTTP result (200, 404, 500…), meaningful from state 2 onwards. Success means readyState === 4 and a 2xx status. status === 0 means a network error, a CORS block, or an aborted request.
fetch vs XMLHttpRequest — key differences and gotchas?

fetch is promise-based and cleaner, supports streaming bodies, works with Service Workers, and uses Request/Response objects. Gotchas: it doesn't reject on HTTP errors (only on network failures), so always check res.ok. Cookies aren't sent cross-origin unless you set credentials:'include'. There's no built-in timeout (use AbortSignal.timeout()), and no upload progress events. XHR still wins for upload progress.
What is the Same-Origin Policy and how does CORS relax it?

The browser stops JS on origin A (scheme + host + port) from reading responses from origin B. CORS is the server opting in through response headers: Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods, -Headers, -Credentials. "Non-simple" requests (PUT or DELETE, Content-Type: application/json, custom headers like Authorization) trigger an OPTIONS preflight first. CORS is enforced by the browser only: Postman and server-to-server calls ignore it. With credentials, the allowed origin can't be *.
How do you send the CSRF token with AJAX to Spring Security?

For cookie or session-based apps, Spring expects the token in a header such as X-CSRF-TOKEN or X-XSRF-TOKEN. Option 1: render <meta name="_csrf" content="${_csrf.token}"> and copy it into every request ($.ajaxSetup or a fetch wrapper). Option 2: CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse() writes an XSRF-TOKEN cookie, which JS reads and sends back as X-XSRF-TOKEN. Angular's HttpClient does this automatically. Stateless JWT APIs usually disable CSRF.
What data formats can AJAX use? Why JSON over XML?

JSON, XML, HTML fragments, plain text, binary (Blob or ArrayBuffer), and FormData/multipart. JSON won because it maps directly onto JS objects (JSON.parse), is lighter than XML, easy to read, and supported everywhere (Jackson on the Spring side). JSONP was an old hack for cross-domain GETs using a script tag. It's insecure, so use CORS instead.
How do you avoid race conditions with AJAX (e.g. a search box)?

Responses can arrive out of order, so a slow reply for "an" can overwrite the result for "ang". Fixes: abort the previous request (AbortController, jqXHR.abort()), or ignore stale responses using a request counter. In Angular, switchMap does this automatically. Add debounce so you don't send a request on every keystroke.
How do you handle errors, loading state and retries in AJAX?

Show a spinner and disable the button while the request is in flight, and hide it in finally. Separate network errors (offline, CORS, timeout) from HTTP errors (4xx means show a validation message, 401 means redirect to login, 5xx means show a "try again" message). Retry only idempotent requests, with exponential backoff. Show the server's error details, such as a ProblemDetail detail field, to the user.
Is AJAX bad for SEO / browser history? How do SPAs fix it?

Content loaded by JS might not be indexed, and AJAX navigation doesn't change the URL, so Back and bookmarks break. Fixes: the History API (pushState, popstate) or a router (Angular Router) for real URLs, plus SSR or pre-rendering (Angular SSR, hydration) so crawlers see the content.
Polling vs long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket — which one when?

Polling is the simplest but wasteful. Long polling is a fallback. SSE is server-to-client only, uses plain HTTP, reconnects automatically, and is ideal for notifications and progress. WebSocket is bidirectional and low-latency, for chat and collaboration, but needs stateful connections and more infrastructure work (sticky sessions or a message broker for scaling).
Does a failed CORS check stop the request from reaching the server?

It depends. For a preflighted request, a failed preflight means the real request is never sent. For a simple request, such as a form-encoded POST, the server receives and executes it, and the browser merely stops JS reading the response. So CORS is not a server-side protection and must not be used in place of authentication or CSRF defences.
I see "CORS error" in the console, but Postman works. Walk through the fix.

- Look in the Network tab for the OPTIONS request and its status.
- A 401 or 403 on OPTIONS: Spring Security is blocking it. Use http.cors(...).
- A 200 with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin: the origin in the config does not match exactly (scheme, host and port all count).
- A wildcard with credentials: set an explicit origin, and allowCredentials(true).
- A proxy or gateway may strip the headers, or add them twice; a duplicate header value also fails.
- A 500 on the actual request often shows as a CORS error, since error responses may lack the headers.
Postman ignores CORS, so it only proves the API works.
What is res.ok for a 304, 301 or 404?

res.ok is true only for status 200 to 299. A 404 resolves with ok === false. A 301 is followed automatically, so you see the final response, with res.redirected === true. A revalidated 304 is turned into a 200 from cache. fetch rejects only when no HTTP response was obtained: DNS failure, refused connection, CORS block or abort.
What do you do if two parts of the code need to read the same fetch Response?

The body is a stream and can be consumed once, so a second read throws a TypeError. Call res.clone() before reading. A service worker's cache-and-return flow is the classic case: cache.put(req, res.clone()); return res;. Cloning a large streamed response buffers data in memory, so read once and pass the parsed value around if you can.
How do you show upload progress and download progress?

Upload: use XHR's xhr.upload.onprogress, since standard fetch has no upload progress event. In Angular, use reportProgress: true with the XHR backend. Download: fetch can do it by reading res.body chunks and comparing the bytes read with Content-Length. That header is missing when compressed or chunked, so show an indeterminate spinner in that case.
Which methods are safe to retry automatically?

GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition, so they can be retried on a network failure or 503. POST is not, as a lost response does not tell you whether the server acted, and a retry could create a duplicate order. Make POST safe by sending an Idempotency-Key header that the server stores with the result. Do not retry 4xx, except for 408 and 429, and honour Retry-After. Add jitter to avoid many clients retrying at the same moment.
What is JSONP, exactly, and why was it dangerous?

A <script> tag is not restricted by the Same-Origin Policy. JSONP loads /api?callback=cb, and the server responds with JavaScript: cb({"a":1}), which then runs. It supports only GET, has no proper error handling, and gives the remote server full script execution in your page. Spring removed its JSONP support. CORS replaced it.
Offset vs cursor pagination for an infinite scroll?

With offset (?page=3, LIMIT 20 OFFSET 60), the database still scans skipped rows, so deep pages are slow, and rows inserted during scrolling produce duplicates or gaps. With a cursor (?after=lastId, WHERE id > ?), each page uses the index, so it is fast at any depth and stable under inserts, but you cannot jump to page 50. Use a cursor for feeds and offset for admin tables with page numbers.
How do you avoid request waterfalls and duplicate calls on a page?

Send independent requests in parallel with Promise.all or forkJoin. Share an in-flight request: keep a Map of URL to promise, return the same promise while it is pending, and remove it when settled. Cache results with a short lifetime. On the API side, an aggregate endpoint or a Backend-for-Frontend replaces many calls with one. HTTP/2 allows many parallel streams over one connection, while HTTP/1.1 browsers limit each origin to about six connections.
Scenario: you get 401 on a call, refresh the token, and repeat. What can go wrong?

Several requests fail together and each one starts its own refresh. With rotating refresh tokens, the second refresh uses a token that has already been consumed, and the user is logged out. Keep a single shared refresh promise: the first 401 starts it, and the others await it, then retry once. Exclude the refresh endpoint from this logic, otherwise a failure loops forever. Limit each request to one retry. If the refresh fails, clear state and go to login.
Is it safe to insert an AJAX response with innerHTML?

Not when it holds user-supplied data. Stored values such as a name of become script execution, which is stored XSS. Use textContent or a framework's binding, or sanitise with DOMPurify if HTML is required. Encode values placed in URLs with encodeURIComponent. On the server, send correct Content-Type headers, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so JSON is never interpreted as HTML.
What's a CSRF risk with AJAX if the API uses cookies?

The browser sends cookies with cross-site requests in some cases, so another site can trigger a state-changing call even though it cannot read the response. A JSON content type gives some protection through preflight, but that is not a design you should rely on. Use SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies, plus a CSRF token, and check the Origin header. A fetch with Authorization: Bearer from memory is not CSRF-prone, since browsers do not attach that automatically.
The file downloads but is named "download" or the header is null. Why?

On a cross-origin call, JavaScript can only read a small list of "CORS-safelisted" response headers (such as Content-Type). Content-Disposition is not on it, so res.headers.get('Content-Disposition') returns null until the server adds Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Content-Disposition (in Spring: exposedHeaders("Content-Disposition")). The same applies to custom headers like X-Total-Count used for pagination.
How do you send a JWT with EventSource (SSE)?

You cannot: EventSource does not allow custom headers. Options: use cookie authentication (same-site, with withCredentials: true for cross-origin), pass a short-lived, single-use token in the query string (never the main access token, since URLs end up in logs), or use fetch with a streaming res.body reader and parse the SSE format yourself, which supports headers and POST bodies. The fetch approach loses automatic reconnection, so you add that yourself.
Why do WebSocket messages reach only some users when the app runs on two servers?

Each WebSocket connection is pinned to one server instance. With Spring's in-memory simple broker, a message published on instance A is delivered only to clients connected to A. Fix it with a broker relay (enableStompBrokerRelay to RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ) or a pub/sub layer such as Redis that fans messages out to all instances. Sticky sessions on the load balancer keep a client on one instance but do not solve fan-out.
REST vs GraphQL from the front-end point of view?

REST: one URL per resource, HTTP caching and status codes work naturally, simple to secure and monitor; but a screen may need several calls (under-fetching) or get fields it does not use (over-fetching). GraphQL: one endpoint, the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one round trip, with a typed schema; but HTTP caching is harder (usually POST), errors often come back with status 200 in an errors array, and the server must guard against expensive queries. Spring supports it via Spring for GraphQL. Choose GraphQL when many different clients need different shapes of the same data.
What does a 204 No Content mean for your fetch code?

res.ok is true, but there is no body, so await res.json() throws a SyntaxError. Check res.status === 204 (or the Content-Length) before parsing. Spring returns 204 from ResponseEntity.noContent().build() or a void method annotated @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT), which is common for DELETE.
How do you send an array or a list of IDs to a Spring @RequestParam?

Spring binds repeated parameters or a comma list to List<Long> ids: ?ids=1&ids=2 or ?ids=1,2. Build it with URLSearchParams: ids.forEach(id => params.append('ids', id)). Avoid the bracket style ids[]=1 that some libraries produce by default (jQuery without traditional: true, some Axios serializers). For long lists, use a POST with a JSON body to stay under URL length limits.
